refs.title: The test
refs.notes: The test I and many aging scientists settled on: DunedinPACE. It estimates the speed your body is aging. 1.0 means one year per calendar year. My best score was 0.65; the average of my three tests is 0.665. So I age about 6.5 years while the typical person ages 10. Built at Duke and Columbia from the Dunedin, New Zealand cohort followed since birth; published 2022; used in 65+ large studies in 18 countries. Nature Aging 2024: faster pace predicted shorter healthspans and lives. The part ads leave out: my score went back up to 0.76 after supplement mistakes and a chaotic menopausal stretch. Testing again at year end. One test, one person, one body: a story, not a clinical trial.

refs.title: The icing
refs.notes: Why start with the icing? Because it is everywhere and makes people feel behind. Affordable on the left: sauna, prebiotics, most supplements. Real money as you move right: NAD drips, peptides, stem cells, hyperbaric oxygen, rapamycin. At the far end a program costing about two million dollars a year with a medical team and blood transfusions. I am not saying don’t. I am saying not first. Nobody in the blue zones is in a hyperbaric chamber. What I do: a tested longevity supplement combination and sauna three to five days a week; the sauna is what gets me out of bed. Finnish data 2024: 2,575 men, 28 years; four to seven sessions a week, about 40 percent lower all-cause mortality than once a week. The coin on the far left is me: twelve dollars a day.

refs.title: Sleep
refs.notes: Bottom of the cake: sleep, the night shift. Your brain has a drainage system that flushes the day’s waste, mostly while you sleep: the glymphatic system, imaged in living people for the first time by OHSU in 2024. No middle-of-the-night shame spirals; I have had insomnia. Focus on what we control: timing and routine. 2023, 60,000-plus adults: sleep regularity predicted lifespan better than duration; the most regular sleepers had up to 48 percent lower mortality risk. My routine: last meal three hours before bed, ten-minute walk, screens off an hour before, brush, floss, wash, eye mask, cool room. Target window 9 PM to 5 AM. Borrow the order and the consistency, not my clock.

refs.title: Sugar
refs.notes: Sugar and glycemic stability. What we subtract matters as much as what we add. Three words: spike, signal, scar. Spike: what the monitor shows after sugar or simple carbs. Signal: a flood of insulin; locked on high all day, your cells become a garage that never gets cleaned out; chronic over-signaling is a hallmark of aging. Scar: glycation; sugar cross-links collagen and elastin; wrinkles are the visible proof, arteries, eyes and kidneys the invisible one. HbA1c measures sugar stuck to protein. UCSF 2024: 342 women around forty; every gram of added sugar came with an older biological age; they averaged 61 grams a day. BMJ review: keep added sugar under 25 grams, about six teaspoons. Birthday cake stays. Confession: pizza barely moved my monitor; my greens latte spiked it. Every Academy student wears a monitor for two weeks.

refs.title: Same age
refs.notes: Third layer: movement. One picture of why it matters: two people, the same age in calendar years. One strong, one on a walker. Mayo Clinic, December 2024, 183 countries: the gap between how long we live and how long we live in good health. Worldwide 9.6 years. United States 12.4 years, the widest gap in the world. I am in the middle of this with my parents: a decade of not getting to the store or the bathroom alone, losing email and the phone, forgetting finances and grandchildren, falling at night. Not everything is escapable. But exercise is the single most powerful intervention we have. Can we shrink that window to almost nothing? What movement?

refs.title: Movement portfolio
refs.notes: I think of exercise like an investment portfolio. One stock is not diversified, it is optimistic. Four areas. Weights: resistance training, compound lifts; for muscles, bones and increasingly the brain. VO2 max: how much oxygen you can use working hard; declines with age even in elite athletes; hard intervals plus recovery; for heart and lungs. Zone 2: conversational-pace cardio, walking, hiking; metabolic health and heart. Mobility and balance: full range of motion and steadiness; for the brain and the safety to keep doing the other three. Runners add weights and mobility; lifters add cardio and yoga. Data: grip strength tracks mortality almost in a straight line across 48 studies and three million people. 7,000 steps versus 2,000: 47 percent lower mortality, 38 percent lower dementia; not ten thousand. Mayo 2024: the one-leg stand fell fastest with age. Tonight: shoes off, non-dominant leg, aim for thirty seconds.

refs.title: Movement week
refs.notes: That is what my week looks like. How do you fit all this in? I did not build it in a day: twenty-five years of adding, subtracting and fine-tuning. Travel and deadlines change it, but the bones stay. It is an example of a diversified portfolio, not a test to pass tomorrow. Start small: short movement breaks, a few sets of air squats through the day, cut post-meal glucose spikes by over twenty percent; big leg muscles pull glucose straight out of the blood. A daily walk and air squats while the coffee brews is a very respectable start. Check with your doctor if you need to. The goal is to start moving.

refs.title: Stress
refs.notes: The fourth layer is the one almost everyone skips. I hate the phrase stress management; it sounds like an HR seminar. But stress is the silent saboteur: pristine diet, all the weights, 7,000 steps, and elevated cortisol undoes it from the inside. 2018, a stressful divorce: my cortisol curve was inverted, rock bottom in the morning, spiking at night. Supplements are a band-aid. I learned Transcendental Meditation; six months later the curve had normalized and has stayed that way. TM is not magic; breathwork, mindfulness, prayer, meditation all trigger the same reset. The best practice is the one you will do. Free five-minute tool: the physiological sigh, Stanford: five minutes a day improved mood and calmed the nervous system faster than standard meditation. Double inhale through the nose, long slow exhale through the mouth. Three together, now.

refs.title: The protocol
refs.notes: All four layers in a single day, so you can see where they fight for the same hour. 5 AM wake, water, prayer, light. 7 AM movement and sauna. 8 AM eating window opens: greens, protein, fiber, fruit. 9 AM caffeine cut-off. Eating window 8 to 6, ten hours: constraining eating to 8 to 10 hours improved blood sugar and body fat without changing what people ate; earlier windows do even better. Midday main meal and a walk. 1 PM stress reset. 6 PM kitchen closes, three hours before bed. 8 PM screens off. 9 PM lights out. Notice: the whole day is built backward from bedtime. Lights out at nine sets dinner at six; dinner at six sets the window opening at eight. Sleep is the master foundation. Life wins sometimes; I reset the next morning. What transfers is the order of operations: sleep, then food, movement, stress. My 5 AM might be your 6:30. Screenshot this slide and pick one or two anchors.

refs.title: Test then buy
refs.notes: Tracking does not have to be expensive. Almost every layer shows up in a number you can measure with a pencil, a notebook, a modest watch or scale: steps, resting heart rate, sleep duration, blood pressure. The goal is to stop guessing. Supplements: the best advice is not a list. My stack is tailored to my body, genetics and blood work; yours should be too. Work with your physician or a functional medicine doctor to see your baseline: vitamin D, homocysteine, inflammatory markers, micronutrients. Test first, then targeted buying. A blood test tells you where the cake has a hole so you know where to put the icing. What I take, as one example: D3 with K2; magnesium taurate, malate and glycinate; B-complex; omega-3s; NOVOS, which I have an affiliate account with. Full breakdown at JulieGibsonClark.com. refs.title: Three questions
refs.notes: That is the cake. Numbers are not what kept me showing up for twenty-five years. Three questions did. Intention: the sentence on the wall. Mine: I want my healthspan to match my lifespan; drag the second line up to meet the first. Why: the feeling behind it, the engine that keeps you going when protocols become routine. Mine: being here to show my son a different possibility for how we age, and keeping Parkinson’s and dementia far away. Resources: time, energy, money, relationships, the real amounts. Mine: about an hour in the morning and twelve dollars a day. Resources filter out the adverts. No million-dollar budget? Great: let go of peptides and stem cells and focus on a solid gym routine. Friends who want this too? Start a group. When all three align you stop asking what should I do and start asking does this fit. A sauna session fits. A 9 PM bedtime fits. Not willpower: three honest questions doing the heavy lifting.
